# Diagnosing Intermittent Fuel Starvation in Small Engines

When a small engine like the Briggs & Stratton found in a Kraftsman 550 series push mower runs for roughly ten minutes before sputtering and dying, you are looking at a classic fuel starvation or air leak scenario. The fact that each restart results in a shorter runtime is the critical diagnostic clue. If this were purely an ignition issue, such as a failing magneto coil, the engine would likely fail to restart entirely or run no more than one cycle. A progressive decline in running time indicates that the system has a finite reservoir of combustible mixture that depletes faster and faster with every attempt, or that a vacuum seal is breaking down under load.

You have already performed the standard maintenance: cleaning the carburetor, replacing the fuel tank cap gasket (by loosening the cap), swapping the spark plug, changing the blade, and replacing the diaphragm in the primer bulb assembly. Since these steps did not resolve the issue, we need to look deeper into the fuel delivery path and potential vapor lock conditions.

One of the most common overlooked culprits in this specific symptom profile is a clogged fuel filter or a restriction within the fuel line itself. Even if you cleaned the carburetor jets, the volume of fuel required over ten minutes might exceed what the tank can supply through a restricted line. When the engine is running, it creates a vacuum in the carburetor bowl to draw fuel up from the tank. If there is significant resistance—perhaps a kinked line, a collapsed hose due to age, or a debris blockage further down the line—the pump (or gravity feed) struggles to keep up as the engine warms and expands components slightly.

Consider the physics of the setup. The fuel tank relies on atmospheric pressure pushing down on the liquid to force it into the carburetor float bowl. If the venting system is compromised, a vacuum can form in the tank itself, preventing further flow regardless of how clean your carburetor is. While you mentioned trying loosening the cap when it sputters, which temporarily relieves the pressure differential, this confirms that airflow to the tank is insufficient. However, simply relying on that workaround isn't sustainable; the root cause remains a blocked air passage or a restricted fuel line.

Another possibility specific to older Briggs & Stratton engines involves the primer bulb and its associated check valves. You replaced the diaphragm, but were you also inspecting the small internal flapper valves inside the primer assembly? If those one-way valves are sticky or leaking slightly in reverse, air can be drawn back into the tank during operation, creating a vacuum lock that worsens with every minute of running time. This explains why the runtime decreases incrementally; each cycle pulls more air out of the system before it can restart properly.

To troubleshoot this effectively, I recommend removing the fuel line at the carburetor inlet and blowing compressed air through it to check for restrictions. If the flow is sluggish, replace the entire hose rather than just cleaning it. You should also verify that the fuel tank vent hole (usually located in the cap or a separate tube) is not obstructed by debris from the tank bottom.

If the mechanical checks come up clean, the issue may lie with the carburetor float level. A float that sits too high can prevent enough fuel from entering the bowl to sustain operation under load, causing the engine to starve once it reaches a certain RPM or throttle position. Adjusting the needle screw on the carburetor can sometimes compensate for this, but physically measuring the float height against the manufacturer's specification is more accurate.
